content: Green-aviation research on battery and alternative-fuel chemistries has advanced rapidly, but a persistent blind spot remains: the psychological readiness of the maintenance personnel who operate these systems daily under safety-critical conditions.Silver-zinc (Ag-Zn) batteries, used in fighter aircraft for their high energy density, evolve hydrogen and oxygen gas through electrolysis of their alkaline electrolyte during charging -a hazard that builds invisibly over 36-to-72-hour charge cycles and becomes dangerous only once hydrogen concentration crosses its lower explosion limit.Managing this hazard depends less on chemistry knowledge and more on sustained technician vigilance during a long, low-stimulation monitoring task -precisely the condition under which classic vigilancedecrement research shows attentional lapses emerge, independent of training or competence.Drawing on the author's two decades as an aviation electrical maintenance engineer and a second career in applied and clinical psychology within the same defence environment, this paper argues that emerging green-energy-storage chemistries (lithium-ion, solidstate, hydrogen fuel cells) will introduce comparable low-visibility, highconsequence hazards, and that maintenance-crew psychological readiness must be engineered alongside the chemistry itself.Integrating self-efficacy theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and vigilance-decrement research, the paper proposes a Psychology-Chemistry Interface Model with three components -chemistry-literacy calibration, hazardtolerability screening, and stress-buffered reporting culture -and a training framework for building calibrated, sustained vigilance in ground crews adopting new energy chemistries, including a low-cost toolkit -a pre-task hazard card, a vigilance-rotation roster, a hazard-tolerability selfcheck, and an added prompt within existing incident-reporting procedures -deployable at a single maintenance unit without new infrastructure.

title: Integrating Geological Research and Environmental Monitoring in Mineral Extraction: A Critical Review of Frameworks, Technologies and Research Priorities
source: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science and Technology
summary: Mineral extraction is expanding to supply the materials required for the energy transition, while ore grades decline and the volumes of waste per unit of metal rise.These trends increase the environmental consequences of mining and make the
content: Mineral extraction is expanding to supply the materials required for the energy transition, while ore grades decline and the volumes of waste per unit of metal rise.These trends increase the environmental consequences of mining and make the traditional separation between geological investigation (exploration, resource modelling) and environmental monitoring (compliance sampling, post-hoc assessment) increasingly untenable.This review synthesises the literature on how geological knowledge and environmental monitoring can be integrated across the mine life cycle.We first summarise the geological controls on environmental risk, including deposit type, mineralogy, geochemical background and the prediction of acid and metalliferous drainage.We then review the monitoring toolbox: geochemical and hydrogeochemical sampling, portable analytical methods, geophysical imaging, optical and radar remote sensing, high-frequency sensors and DNA-based biomonitoring.Integration frameworks are examined, covering geoenvironmental models, geometallurgical and geoenvironmental block models, data-driven and machine-learning approaches, and early-warning systems for tailings and slope stability, illustrated with the Brumadinho, Tisza and Amazonian gold-mining cases.We discuss governance, datastandardisation and scale-mismatch barriers, and propose a research agenda centred on shared geo-environmental data infrastructure, uncertainty-aware prediction and closure-oriented monitoring design.The review argues that environmental performance is largely determined by geology that is already known, or knowable, at the exploration stage, and that monitoring is most effective when designed from the same geological model that guides extraction.

title: Green Chemistry for Environmental Protection: Molecular Strategies for Plastic, Water and Air Pollution Control
source: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science and Technology
summary: Green chemistry protects the environment by preventing hazardous substances and waste at the molecular level rather than relying only on end-of-pipe treatment.This review examines chemical strategies for plastic, water and air pollution, em
content: Green chemistry protects the environment by preventing hazardous substances and waste at the molecular level rather than relying only on end-of-pipe treatment.This review examines chemical strategies for plastic, water and air pollution, emphasizing catalysis, safer media, renewable feedstocks, selective conversion and resource recovery.Plastic chemistry is discussed through PET hydrolysis, alcoholysis, hydrogenolysis, photoreforming and enzymatic cleavage.Water treatment focuses on Fenton/photo-Fenton chemistry, photocatalytic advanced oxidation, electrochemical oxidation and persulfate activation.Airpollution control is considered through catalytic VOC oxidation, selective catalytic reduction/oxidation and photocatalytic NOx removal.Emerging methods-including biocatalysis, deep eutectic solvents, microwave synthesis, photocatalysis, continuous flow and high-pressure activationare evaluated using atom economy, E-factor, process mass intensity and energy demand.Literature indicates that the strongest approaches combine pollution prevention, catalytic selectivity and recovery.Key challenges remain catalyst durability, mixed waste, transformation-product toxicity, separation energy, scale-up and life-cycle impacts.

title: Bio-Inspired Nanozyme-Mediated Sunlight-Driven Oxygen Activation for Surface Engineering of Polypropylene toward Enhanced Biodegradation
source: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science and Technology
summary: The persistence of synthetic plastics in the environment is largely associated with their chemical stability, hydrophobicity, and resistance to biological attack.Polypropylene (PP), in particular, possesses a chemically stable hydrocarbon b
content: The persistence of synthetic plastics in the environment is largely associated with their chemical stability, hydrophobicity, and resistance to biological attack.Polypropylene (PP), in particular, possesses a chemically stable hydrocarbon backbone that limits its accessibility to microbial transformation.In this study, a bio-inspired nanozyme-mediated, sunlightdriven oxygen-activation strategy was investigated as a surfaceengineering approach to improve the biological accessibility of polypropylene.The experimental system combined sunlight irradiation, molecular oxygen, and a redox-active nanozyme to promote interfacial oxidative modification of PP.Polypropylene coupons were subjected to six experimental conditions: untreated PP (C1), sunlight treatment (C2), nanozyme treatment under dark conditions (C3), sunlight-assisted nanozyme treatment (C4), sunlight-assisted nanozyme treatment under reduced-oxygen conditions (C5), and sunlight-assisted nanozyme treatment in the presence of a reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenger (C6).The treated samples were evaluated using ROS analysis, Fouriertransform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), water contact-angle measurements, and microbial attachment analysis.Molecular-weight analysis was considered a complementary endpoint for evaluating polymer-chain transformation.The combined sunlight-nanozyme treatment produced the highest ROS response and was associated with increased carbonyl functionality and surface oxygen content, a decreased water contact angle, and pronounced surface morphological modifications.Microbial attachment was also higher on the treated PP surface than on untreated PP.These findings indicated that sunlight-assisted nanozyme treatment promoted oxidative modification of the polypropylene interface and increased its biological accessibility.However, surface oxidation,

title: Low-pressure subsurface porous diffuser irrigation system for kitchen wastewater reuse in urban vegetable cultivation: A review of hydraulics, clogging, and automation
summary: By 2050, up to 2.4 billion people are expected to be affected by urban water scarcity, which has led to an interest in reuse of kitchen wastewater, as a low-cost irrigation resource. Previous research has shown that clay pot irrigation is a
content: By 2050, up to 2.4 billion people are expected to be affected by urban water scarcity, which has led to an interest in reuse of kitchen wastewater, as a low-cost irrigation resource. Previous research has shown that clay pot irrigation is a traditional water use efficient irrigation method that can be used with moderately saline water and is several times more efficient than conventional irrigation. This review aims to compile the latest literature on the hydraulics, clogging, and Internet of Things (IoT) based automation of such systems for urban vegetable production using kitchen wastewater. Seepage rates have been previously determined under clean water conditions and simple pretreatment has been found to significantly reduce organic and solid loads. But previous clogging tests, which were mostly conducted with saline, sediment laden or synthetic wastewater, not with real kitchen wastewater, have shown that hydraulic degradation is very severe under poor water quality, which is why pretreatment, is necessary. Earlier research on IoT integration shows that low-cost reference pot level sensing loops can be used to automate refilling, but they are not able to detect individual emitter clogging. Favorable yield and water productivity gains have been reported in prior agronomic and economic studies, but not under actual kitchen wastewater. Together, these results suggest technical feasibility and highlight key areas of long-term hydraulic, agronomic, and economic validation that require integrated field testing prior to household-scale adoption.

title: Active conservation of biodiversity in Italy: conflict or synergy? A comparative analysis between the Italian National Forest Strategy and the National Biodiversity Strategy 2030
source: Forest - Rivista di Selvicoltura ed Ecologia Forestale
summary: We investigated the degree of strategic coherence between the Italian National Forest Strategy and the National Biodiversity Strategy 2030, focusing on how conservation and active forest management are framed within national governance. A q
content: We investigated the degree of strategic coherence between the Italian National Forest Strategy and the National Biodiversity Strategy 2030, focusing on how conservation and active forest management are framed within national governance. A qualitative two-level analysis was conducted. First, we examined the overall architecture of both strategies, including vision, objectives, governance models, implementation tools, and monitoring systems. Second, we performed a thematic comparative assessment across nine policy domains relevant to forest conservation and management. For each domain, we assigned a coherence score ranging from 0 (no convergence) to 5 (full convergence) based on explicit content analysis. Results indicate generally high strategic alignment. Coherence scores ranged from 2 (partial convergence) to 5 (full convergence), with most domains scoring between 3 and 4, indicating good to high convergence. Strong alignment emerged in ecological restoration, ecosystem services, old-growth forest protection, and research and monitoring systems. Lower scores were associated with domains where productive forest use, bioeconomy development, and the degree of active intervention diverge in emphasis. These findings suggest that the two strategies are broadly complementary at the programmatic level, supporting a model of active conservation that integrates biodiversity protection with sustainable forest management. However, differences in governance structure and operational priorities highlight the need for stronger coordination during regional implementation to ensure consistent ecological outcomes.

title: Post-flood contrasts in soil properties and enzyme activities in a karst riparian zone: a paired-block comparative study
summary: Flooding is a primary riparian disturbance, yet the short-term biogeochemical consequences of rare, extreme floods remain poorly characterized in karst floodplains. After a 1-in-50-year flood in a karst reach of the Qingshui River (Guizhou,
content: Flooding is a primary riparian disturbance, yet the short-term biogeochemical consequences of rare, extreme floods remain poorly characterized in karst floodplains. After a 1-in-50-year flood in a karst reach of the Qingshui River (Guizhou, China), we compared soil physicochemical properties, carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P) contents, and potential extracellular enzyme activities between three flood-affected locations covered by freshly deposited silt and three adjacent reference locations. Each flood–reference pair formed one block, yielding 72 observations (three blocks × two conditions × two layers × six dates). In mineral soil, flood-affected locations had higher moisture, organic C, total N, total P, and dissolved organic C, and lower nitrate and nitrite. Potential activities of C-, N-, and P-acquiring hydrolytic enzymes were lower, whereas peroxidase and polyphenol oxidase potentials were higher in both layers. Because cover-layer materials differed (flood silt versus native litter), primary inference uses mineral soil. PLS-SEM path coefficients had 95% bootstrap confidence intervals that included zero, so the path models describe association structure. Vector angles were 37.6° with urease alone and 59.7° with denitrification reductases included, indicating N and P limitation, respectively. These contrasts apply to the studied reach; broader inference requires replicated reaches.

title: Osmotic adjustment, toxic ion exclusion and oxidative protection as key traits for the tolerance to NaCl stress in forage sorghum
summary: This study evaluated the physiological and biochemical responses of two forage sorghum types with contrasting agronomic and genotypic traits, the genotype CSF20 and the variety Catissorgo, under mild salinity stress. Compared with the contr
content: This study evaluated the physiological and biochemical responses of two forage sorghum types with contrasting agronomic and genotypic traits, the genotype CSF20 and the variety Catissorgo, under mild salinity stress. Compared with the control plants, salinity induced a greater reduction in the growth of CSF20 (salt-sensitive) than of Catissorgo (salt-tolerant). Moreover, leaves of CSF20 showed water imbalance and oxidative damage under salt stress. K + remained unaltered in CSF20 tissues but decreased in stems and roots of Catissorgo. Na + and Cl – increased in the aerial tissues and roots. However, lower accumulation in young leaves and stems as well as greater root retention were observed in the salt-tolerant sorghum. Osmotic adjustment was observed in the leaves and roots of Catissorgo, whereas it occurred only in the leaves of CSF20. Cl and Na + contributed to the reduction of osmotic potential in mature leaves of Catissorgo, while Na + was the predominant inorganic osmolyte in CSF20. Organic solutes contributed similarly to the osmotic potential in control and salt-stressed plants; with glucose being the major organic osmolyte. The activities of guaiacol peroxidase and catalase were consistently higher in the leaves of the salt-tolerant sorghum. Salt stress induced the superoxide dismutase activity only in the tolerant sorghum leaves, correlating weakly with the low malondialdehyde accumulation. Overall, differences in salt tolerance between the two forage sorghum types were subtle. Nevertheless, Catissorgo exhibited more robust tolerance mechanisms related to systemic osmotic adjustment, antioxidant protection, and restricted Na + and Cl − transport to shoots than CSF20, which may improve its performance in salinized soils.

title: Depth-Dependent eDNA Abundances across Ecosystems Inform Deep-Sea Sampling Strategies
summary: Environmental DNA (eDNA) surveys are increasingly used to assess marine biodiversity and inform deep-sea environmental decision-making, including mineral resource management and fisheries oversight. Yet standard low-volume protocols inherit
content: Environmental DNA (eDNA) surveys are increasingly used to assess marine biodiversity and inform deep-sea environmental decision-making, including mineral resource management and fisheries oversight. Yet standard low-volume protocols inherited from coastal work may be inadequate at depth, and recent findings indicate that depth- and productivity-aware sampling, often requiring high-volume in situ filtration, is needed. Currently no quantitative framework links depth and ecosystem context to define defensible filtration volume targets. We compiled 841 eDNA samples from eight expeditions across the North Atlantic, Wider Caribbean Region, and Pacific (surface to 4000 m) to quantify how recoverable eDNA scales with depth and surface productivity, and to derive depth- and productivity-aware sampling targets. Total eDNA concentration declined with depth as a power law, with attenuation exponents (b) modulated by surface productivity: most gradual in eutrophic waters (b = 0.67), intermediate in mesotrophic (b = 0.90), and steepest in oligotrophic systems (b = 1.25). Volume-weighted models explained 66–88% of the variance. At a fixed extract-concentration target, required filtration volumes diverged ∼7-fold between oligotrophic and eutrophic systems at 200 m and ∼38-fold at 4000 m. Conventional Niskin sampling therefore undersamples deep-sea animal eDNA, particularly in mid- to low-productivity systems. Among laboratory parameters, the assay-specific extract-concentration target exerted greater leverage on required volume than extraction efficiency or elution volume. Volume-aware sampling paired with optimized recovery should be routine in deep-sea eDNA surveys.

title: Atmospheric Oxidative Capacity Over Heterogeneous Coastal Urban Surfaces in the Greater Houston Metropolitan Area
summary: Atmospheric oxidative capacity (AOC) is a key indicator of the atmosphere's ability to remove pollutants, yet its variability within coastal urban environments remains poorly understood due to complex interactions among emissions, photochem
content: Atmospheric oxidative capacity (AOC) is a key indicator of the atmosphere's ability to remove pollutants, yet its variability within coastal urban environments remains poorly understood due to complex interactions among emissions, photochemistry, and planetary boundary layer (PBL) dynamics. Limited oxidant observations also hinder understanding of atmospheric chemistry aloft and its influence on surface air quality. Here, we use a high‐resolution large‐eddy simulation configuration of the Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled with Chemistry (WRF‐LES‐Chem) to investigate AOC over the Greater Houston metropolitan region during the NASA TRACER‐AQ campaign. By explicitly resolving turbulence, the model captures interactions between vertical mixing and heterogeneous emissions across urban, industrial, rural, and marine environments. Results show that daytime AOC is dominated by hydroxyl radical (OH) oxidation and closely follows PBL development. Urban‐industrial regions, particularly Central Houston and La Porte, exhibit higher AOC due to elevated nitrogen oxides (NOx) and reactive volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions, forming an AOC‐rich layer (>3.0 × 10 7 molecules cm −3 s −1 ) slightly shallower than the daytime PBL height. In low‐NOx rural Brazoria, enhanced radical self‐reactions suppress OH recycling, with isoprene oxidation being a key contributor to OH reactivity. Over the Gulf, weaker photochemistry and a suppressed marine PBL limit AOC despite enhanced OH production from ozone photolysis in the presence of abundant water vapor. These findings demonstrate strong subregional variability in AOC, highlighting the importance of explicitly resolving PBL turbulence‐chemistry interactions to accurately represent radical cycling and secondary pollutant formation in coastal megacity environments.

title: Marine ecological responses to thermal discharge from nuclear and coal-fired power plants: a review focusing on seawater quality, plankton, and microorganisms
summary: With the rapid expansion of coastal nuclear and coal-fired power plants, the environmental impacts of thermal discharge on adjacent marine ecosystems have become a major concern in environmental science. Unlike previous reviews focusing on
content: With the rapid expansion of coastal nuclear and coal-fired power plants, the environmental impacts of thermal discharge on adjacent marine ecosystems have become a major concern in environmental science. Unlike previous reviews focusing on a single biological group or isolated water-quality parameter, this review integrates physicochemical and biological responses, microbial functional ecology and the microbial loop, identifies candidate indicator taxa and functional traits, compares nuclear and coal-fired effluents, and synthesizes effects on seawater physicochemical properties, plankton community structure, and microbial diversity and function. We distinguish two impact pathways, which are direct entrainment/impingement within once-through cooling systems and in situ warming experienced by organisms in the discharged plume. Chlorination by-products, nutrient enrichment and discharge-modified hydrodynamics are considered because they confound field-derived signals; thus many field patterns are mixed-stressor responses and cannot be attributed to warming alone. Nuclear and coal-fired plants differ in effluent composition, in that nuclear once-through discharges during normal operation are dominated by heated seawater and biocide residues. Many field-observed patterns represent mixed-stressor responses and cannot be attributed to warming alone. Thermal discharge reduces dissolved oxygen and pH, accelerates nutrient cycling, increases pollutant bioavailability, and alters phytoplankton, zooplankton, and microbial communities, thereby affecting food-web stability and biogeochemical processes. The review also discusses current controversies and knowledge gaps. The main contribution of this review is to integrate seawater chemistry, plankton dynamics and microbial functional ecology within a single attribution framework, to identify candidate indicator taxa and functional traits. This synthesis provides a scientific basis for environmental monitoring, ecological risk assessment and adaptive management of thermal discharge in coastal marine ecosystems.

title: Making SDGs Material: A Multi‐Criteria Approach to Harmonize Corporate Social Responsibility Actions With Sustainability Challenges
source: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management
summary: The UN's 2030 Agenda urges companies to prioritize Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). However, balancing competitiveness with stakeholder expectations remains challenging. This study develops a materiality‐based Multi‐Criteria Decision‐M
content: The UN's 2030 Agenda urges companies to prioritize Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). However, balancing competitiveness with stakeholder expectations remains challenging. This study develops a materiality‐based Multi‐Criteria Decision‐Making method to identify SDGs most relevant to the company's context, where materiality is understood, in practical terms, as the process of identifying and prioritizing the sustainability issues that most affect a company's economic, environmental, and social impacts and that most influence stakeholders' assessments and decisions. Grounded in Global Reporting Initiative materiality principles, the method integrates Fuzzy Analytic Network Process and Interval‐Valued Triangular Fuzzy Numbers Additive Ratio Assessment to evaluate sustainability issues across strategic relevance, sustainability performance, and stakeholder expectations. Fuzzy logic mitigates uncertainty and subjectivity, while structured stakeholder engagement ensures multi‐perspective input. Material topics are mapped to SDGs, providing an evidence‐based foundation for Corporate Social Responsibility planning. The method was tested through a pilot application in an Italian SME, a review session with the company's CEO, and consultations with Environmental, Social, and Governance practitioners, which provided initial evidence of its feasibility and practical usefulness; a sensitivity analysis indicated that the resulting SDG ranking is stable within the case examined. The study advances Corporate Social Responsibility and sustainability management literature by operationalizing materiality analysis for SDG prioritization and offers managers a replicable tool to enhance decision transparency and accountability.

title: Anthropogenic noise affects Oikopleura dioica behaviour in a life stage- and signal-dependent manner
summary: Anthropogenic noise is an increasingly important pollutant of marine environments, yet its effects on zooplankton remain poorly understood. The appendicularian Oikopleura dioica is a globally distributed filter-feeding tunicate whose locomo
content: Anthropogenic noise is an increasingly important pollutant of marine environments, yet its effects on zooplankton remain poorly understood. The appendicularian Oikopleura dioica is a globally distributed filter-feeding tunicate whose locomotion and house-building behaviour directly influence feeding efficiency and carbon export. Here, we investigated how anthropogenic noise affects behaviour across the life cycle of O. dioica, from larvae to juveniles and adults, using stage-specific tracking and quantitative behavioural analyses to assess responses to a high-intensity standardized noise band (MSFD-NB) and a vessel-derived noise signal (Vessel-DNS). Animals exhibited consistent behavioural alterations during and after noise exposure, and the responses differed strongly among life stages and between noise signals. Larvae showed the greatest sensitivity, displaying increased locomotor activity and altered movement dynamics during exposure, as well as persistent post-exposure effects. Juveniles exhibited treatment-dependent changes in trajectory organization, whereas adults showed modifications in orientation, turning behaviour, and tail-driven propulsion. In adults residing within their filter-feeding house, noise altered pumping-associated movements without affecting house-expansion frequency. These findings demonstrate that anthropogenic noise impacts behaviour throughout the O. dioica life cycle in a stage- and signal-specific manner, suggesting that noise pollution may not only impact individual performance, but potentially also ecological processes linked to marine food webs, carbon sequestration, and consequently, ocean health.

title: Orbital spectroscopy links dust source composition to atmospheric acidity and nitrate
summary: Mineral dust affects atmospheric chemistry, air quality, and climate, yet its impacts remain uncertain because its mineral composition is poorly constrained. Here we combine NASA EMIT orbital imaging spectroscopy with a satellite-constraine
content: Mineral dust affects atmospheric chemistry, air quality, and climate, yet its impacts remain uncertain because its mineral composition is poorly constrained. Here we combine NASA EMIT orbital imaging spectroscopy with a satellite-constrained global chemistry model to quantify how source-resolved calcite variability alters aerosol chemistry and optical properties. EMIT-derived calcite improves agreement with airborne observations and reveals contrasts in dust alkalinity. Compared with globally averaged calcite, source-resolved calcite shifts regional annual mean aerosol pH by -0.6 to +0.5 units, with local changes exceeding 1 pH unit across substantial areas of the most affected dust-influenced regions, reaching -4 to +3 units in limited areas. These acidity changes reorganize secondary inorganic aerosol formation, nitrate partitioning, and extreme nitrate events, particularly where dust interacts with anthropogenic pollution. In contrast, calcite-driven secondary-aerosol radiative effects are small relative to those caused by spatial variations in iron-oxide absorption. These results show that calcite variability strongly modulates heterogeneous chemistry, whereas iron oxides dominate radiative impacts.

title: Transcriptomic modulation of biofortified spinach through foliar application of lemon-derived vesicles and nanoencapsulated selenium
summary: Selenium biofortification of crops is an effective strategy to address micronutrient deficiencies, although its efficiency is often limited by suboptimal uptake and phytotoxicity. In this study, we investigated the use of lemon-derived vesi
content: Selenium biofortification of crops is an effective strategy to address micronutrient deficiencies, although its efficiency is often limited by suboptimal uptake and phytotoxicity. In this study, we investigated the use of lemon-derived vesicles as nanocarriers for the foliar delivery of selenate in spinach ( Spinacia oleracea L.), aiming to enhance selenium accumulation while determining its effects on plant physiology. Plants were treated with free or nanoencapsulated selenate, and physiological, metabolic, and transcriptomic responses were evaluated. Nanoencapsulation of selenium in vesicles significantly improved Se accumulation in leaves, resulting in more than twofold increase compared with free selenate application. Molecular analyses revealed that selenium enrichment was associated with the activation of glutathione-related pathways and reduced proline levels. In addition, vesicle application also induced phenylpropanoid metabolism and nutrient reservoir-related genes, alongside changes in redox-related responses. Notably, vesicles alone promoted plant growth, increasing both fresh and dry weight, whereas selenium-loaded vesicles only increased fresh weight. Vesicle application also modulated secondary metabolism, including hesperidin accumulation. These findings suggest that lemon-derived vesicles could serve as an efficient selenium delivery system, offering a promising approach for foliar selenium biofortification of spinach. However, further studies are needed to assess the scalability of this approach, its field performance, and formulation shelf life.

title: Selective calibration of direct OCO-2 level-1B XCO2 retrieval across held-out TCCON stations
summary: Introduction Prescreening, retrieval failure, and quality filtering leave many Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2) soundings without usable estimates of the column-averaged dry-air mole fraction of CO 2 (XCO 2 ). Methods We developed a se
content: Introduction Prescreening, retrieval failure, and quality filtering leave many Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2) soundings without usable estimates of the column-averaged dry-air mole fraction of CO 2 (XCO 2 ). Methods We developed a selective calibration framework to retrieve XCO 2 directly from Level-1B spectra and improve its accuracy at locations outside the training domains. A neural network ensemble learns from quality-filtered Level-2 labels. Predictions with low disagreement across training checkpoints are accepted for residual calibration against measurements from the Total Carbon Column Observing Network (TCCON). We evaluated the framework at seven TCCON stations using leave-one-station-out evaluation and independent annual training for 2020 and 2021. Each target station was withheld from all model development. Results Screening retained 86.7% of matched soundings in 2020 and 89.1% in 2021. On the accepted observations, calibration reduced root mean square error (RMSE), averaged equally across stations, from 2.666 to 1.907 ppm in 2020 and from 3.390 to 2.508 ppm in 2021. RMSE decreased at all seven held-out stations in both years, and the average improvement persisted across all 12 spatial and temporal matching windows. Calibration also improved estimates for soundings without matched Level-2 records, which comprised approximately half of the accepted observations in each year. Discussion These results establish that residual corrections learned at source stations can improve direct retrieval at unseen stations, extending externally evaluated XCO 2 estimates to observations outside the conventional Level-2 population.

title: Global mangrove age structure shapes blue carbon benefits of forest growth and conservation
summary: Forest expansion, growth and loss shape age structure and determine the capacity of forests to retain and accumulate carbon. Understanding these dynamics is particularly important for mangroves, whose conservation is widely promoted as a na
content: Forest expansion, growth and loss shape age structure and determine the capacity of forests to retain and accumulate carbon. Understanding these dynamics is particularly important for mangroves, whose conservation is widely promoted as a natural climate solution, yet their current age structure, its implications for carbon accumulation, and how conservation can enhance this accumulation remain poorly understood. Here we integrated four decades of satellite observations, spaceborne LiDAR measurements, and field-derived allometric equations to map global mangrove stand age and reconstruct spatially-explicit trajectories of aboveground carbon (AGC) accumulation. We show that current global mangrove extent is dominated by mature (≥ 40 years) stands, while younger stands occupy only 12% yet accumulate AGC rapidly at a rate of 3.97 MgC ha-1 yr-1, plateauing at ~28 years. However, the limited extent of young stands and slowing accumulation as they mature constrain projected AGC gains from existing forests to ~9% by 2070 relative to the 2023 baseline of 1.23 PgC. Preventing loss while allowing natural expansion, regeneration and growth, together with active restoration, could increase this gain to ~30% by retaining carbon in mature stands and adding new cohorts. Our findings connect forest demography with conservation outcomes, demonstrating how stand establishment, persistence and growth shape future blue carbon stocks.

title: Crystalline SiO2 modulates molecular hydrogen storage and redistribution in the Earth’s interior
summary: Molecular hydrogen (H 2 ) is increasingly recognized as an important volatile species in Earth's interior, yet the mechanisms governing its storage and transport remain poorly understood. Using high-pressure experiments performed under subd
content: Molecular hydrogen (H 2 ) is increasingly recognized as an important volatile species in Earth's interior, yet the mechanisms governing its storage and transport remain poorly understood. Using high-pressure experiments performed under subduction-zone conditions (1.5–9.6 GPa, 500–950 °C) with externally buffered aqueous fluids (ΔFMQ ≈ −6.0 to +0.4) and analysis of the quenched fluids, we show that crystalline SiO 2 incorporates molecular H 2 through intracrystalline physisorption within its intrinsic structural voids. The equilibrium H 2 uptake is controlled by hydrogen chemical potential and reaches up to ~3000 μg H 2 g⁻¹ SiO 2 in quartz. Changes in pressure, temperature, redox state, fluid conditions, as well as phase transitions modify the equilibrium partitioning of H 2 , promoting its storage or release as geological conditions evolve. Intracrystalline physisorption therefore provides a previously unrecognized mechanism that modulates molecular hydrogen redistribution and redox evolution in Earth's interior.

title: Fireworks promote the secondary formation of atmospheric imidazoles rather than their direct emission: Insights from firework source samples and machine learning
summary: Firework emissions release large quantities of reactive nitrogen‑ and carbon‑containing species that can modify aerosol chemical evolution, yet their impacts on imidazole‑containing particles remain poorly constrained. In this work, single‑
content: Firework emissions release large quantities of reactive nitrogen‑ and carbon‑containing species that can modify aerosol chemical evolution, yet their impacts on imidazole‑containing particles remain poorly constrained. In this work, single‑particle aerosol mass spectrometry was deployed to probe imidazole evolution during the firework (FW) episode in Liaocheng, China, combined with source sample experiments and multi‑model machine learning analysis. Field observations revealed pronounced elevations in particle counts and fractional contributions of imidazoles during the FW episode, along with a shift from bimodal to trimodal particle-size distribution and strengthened internal mixing with sulfate, nitrate, and ammonium. Analysis of firework source samples confirmed no direct imidazole emissions from fireworks, yet abundant precursors of imidazoles (including amines, ammonium, and carbonyl compounds) were detected. Machine learning attribution identified carbonyl compounds and amines as predominant drivers for imidazole formation, with modified particle acidity acting as a secondary modulator, whereas inorganic salts, relative humidity, and NOx exerted largely indirect regulatory effects. Photochemical degradation driven by O3 constituted a major atmospheric sink for imidazoles. This study demonstrates that fireworks predominantly boost the secondary production of imidazoles rather than direct primary emissions, which advances mechanistic insights into episodic brown‑carbon evolution and nitrogen‑heterocycle aerosol pollution driven by intense short‑term combustion events.

title: Calcium–porphyrin metal organic framework/starch hybrid beads for pH-responsive and photostable drug delivery of Nifuroxazide and Omeprazole
summary: Drug-loaded beads have attracted significant interest as advanced delivery systems due to their ability to enhance drug stability, bioavailability, and controlled release. Omeprazole and Nifuroxazide suffer from challenges such as acid degr
content: Drug-loaded beads have attracted significant interest as advanced delivery systems due to their ability to enhance drug stability, bioavailability, and controlled release. Omeprazole and Nifuroxazide suffer from challenges such as acid degradation, poor dissolution, and limited stability, which can reduce their therapeutic effectiveness. Encapsulation within bead-based carriers protects these drugs from gastrointestinal conditions and enables targeted release, thereby improving their overall therapeutic performance. To overcome these drawbacks, this work has engineered a novel oral drug delivery system in the form of a Ca-TCPP/starch bead. This innovative platform leverages the porous structure of the Ca-TCPP material to achieve substantial drug encapsulation and high loading capabilities. In this study, a calcium-tetrakis(4-carboxyphenyl)porphyrin (Ca-TCPP) MOF was successfully synthesized and incorporated into starch-based spherical beads to construct a hybrid inorganic-organic carrier with improved structural stability and controlled release behaviour. Comprehensive characterization using FT-IR, PXRD, SEM, EDX, and BET analyses confirmed the formation of a mesoporous composite featuring uniformly dispersed nanocrystalline MOF domains within the biopolymeric matrix. The Ca-TCPP@starch beads were evaluated as drug delivery vehicles for Nifuroxazide and omeprazole. Both drugs exhibit stability limitations under physiological conditions. The system demonstrated high encapsulation efficiencies across different concentrations (90% for Nifuroxazide and 85% for omeprazole). Kinetic modelling of Nifuroxazide indicated that a zero-order model predominantly governs the release profile, while for omeprazole, the first-order kinetic model yielded the best fit for all formulations. Additionally, photostability investigations showed that the hybrid matrix significantly retards light-induced degradation, particularly for Nifuroxazide, while preserving the pH-dependent stability of omeprazole. Overall, the developed composite integrates high surface area, tunable porosity, and environmental responsiveness within a single platform. These findings highlight the potential of Ca-TCPP MOF-starch hybrids as a versatile system for drug delivery applications demanding controlled release and enhanced chemical protection.

title: Drip irrigation combined with film mulching improves maize yield components and grain nitrogen content by enhancing resource use capacity in arid agricultural region
summary: Introduction Integrating film mulching with irrigation provides a practical approach to improving maize productivity and resource use capacity in irrigated agricultural regions. However, how different film types and irrigation methods joint
content: Introduction Integrating film mulching with irrigation provides a practical approach to improving maize productivity and resource use capacity in irrigated agricultural regions. However, how different film types and irrigation methods jointly regulate soil water dynamics, canopy light utilization, and yield formation remains unclear. Methods Field experiments were conducted during the 2018 and 2019 maize growing seasons in the Hetao Irrigation District, northwestern China. Five management practices were evaluated: CK, TFBI, BFBI, TFDI, and BFDI, corresponding to no mulching with border irrigation, transparent film with border irrigation, black film with border irrigation, transparent film with drip irrigation, and black film with drip irrigation, respectively. We evaluated soil water storage (SWS), leaf area index (LAI), relative chlorophyll content (SPAD), net photosynthetic rate (A), radiation intercept ratio (FIPAR), grain yield, and resource use efficiencies. Results Compared with CK, film mulching under border irrigation increased SWS by 11.40% on average during the maize growing seasons. Compared with BFBI, TFBI further increased LAI, SPAD, and A at tasseling by 5.57%, 6.90%, and 14.35%, respectively. When combined with drip irrigation, film mulching further stabilized root zone water supply and enhanced canopy photosynthetic performance, increasing FIPAR, radiation use efficiency, and biomass (AGB) by 5.09%, 13.30%, and 23.21%, respectively, compared with CK. TFDI produced the highest two-year average grain yield of 14212 kg ha −1 and increased grain nitrogen content, water use efficiency (WUE), and nitrogen partial factor productivity (NPFP) by 26.7%, 89.9%, and 62.5%, respectively, compared with CK. Principal component and correlation analyses showed that yield was mainly associated with AGB, LAI, SPAD, A, FIPAR, WUE, and NPFP. Discussion These results indicate that TFDI enhances maize productivity by optimizing canopy structure, improving photosynthetic capacity, and increasing water and nitrogen use efficiencies. It is an appropriate management model for water-saving and high-yield maize production and efficient resource utilization in arid irrigation areas.

title: Pedogenic Controls on Soil Organic Carbon Persistence in Tropical Soils: A Structured Critical Review with a Colombian Outlook
summary: Tropical soils store large amounts of soil organic carbon (SOC), but the mechanisms governing its persistence vary among mineralogical, hydrological, biological, and geomorphic settings. This structured critical review examines when particu
content: Tropical soils store large amounts of soil organic carbon (SOC), but the mechanisms governing its persistence vary among mineralogical, hydrological, biological, and geomorphic settings. This structured critical review examines when particular processes become limiting for SOC persistence rather than treating soil-forming factors as universal controls. An auditable corpus of 78 unique records was screened using eligibility and evidence-characterization criteria, with 70 records retained for qualitative synthesis. Evidence was evaluated according to study design, environmental context, mechanism, spatial and temporal scale, and inferential directness. Five recurring limiting regimes emerged: carbon-input limitation, microbial-transformation limitation, reactive-mineral-capacity limitation, accessibility limitation associated with aggregation or oxygen restriction, and residence-time limitation associated with vertical or lateral redistribution. Reactive Fe and Al phases can promote mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM) formation when reactive surfaces are accessible and carbon precursors reach them, whereas additional inputs may produce limited MAOM gains when accessible mineral capacity is occupied. Microbial transformation and aggregation act as coupled pathways controlling carbon supply and accessibility, but their effects remain sensitive to nutrient status and disturbance. Redox oscillation, erosion, and hydrological redistribution can alter or override local mineral protection. These boundary conditions help explain contrasting findings across Ferralsols, Acrisols, Andisols, Podzols, savannas, and hydromorphic systems. We propose an operational framework linking mechanisms to measurable indicators, spatial and temporal scales, disturbance tests, and evidence strength, and translate it into a testable Colombian research agenda based on full profiles, pedoclimatic stratification, functional carbon fractions, mineralogy, redox dynamics, and landscape mass balance.

title: Multidirectionally flexible thermoelectric device with conformable phase-change material heatsink for wearable cooling applications
summary: Wearable thermoelectric devices have gained increasing attention for their ability to provide localized temperature regulation through active cooling. Traditional thermoelectric devices (TEDs), often packaged with rigid ceramic components,
content: Wearable thermoelectric devices have gained increasing attention for their ability to provide localized temperature regulation through active cooling. Traditional thermoelectric devices (TEDs), often packaged with rigid ceramic components, face significant challenges in flexibility and adaptability for wearable applications. In this work, we present a highly flexible thermoelectric (TE) module enabled by an engineered copper electrode pattern, together with bismuth telluride–based thermoelectric pillars and an Ecoflex silicone rubber insulating matrix. The engineered electrode pattern enables bending up to approximately 180° in two orthogonal directions while maintaining electrical connectivity. To improve thermal management, a flexible heatsink incorporating aluminum nitride (AlN) and phase-change material (PCM) was integrated with the TE module to form a flexible TED. The integrated device achieved a maximum temperature difference of approximately 12.5 K between its hot and cold sides. Furthermore, a closed-loop proportional–integral–derivative (PID) control system was developed to regulate the cooling-side temperature of the TED. The effects of insulating layer thickness for TE module and different configurations of heatsink, including AlN loading and PCM, were systematically evaluated on cooling duration and temperature regulation under varying temperature conditions. Cooling cycling tests with exchangeable heatsinks further demonstrated repeated cooling operation while maintaining the desired temperature. The bending test was conducted for TE modules with a resistance change of only 2.4% after 1000 bending cycles, indicating good electrical durability. These results demonstrate the combined multidirectional flexibility, temperature-regulated cooling capabilities, and electrical durability of the TED, providing a practical approach toward wearable thermoelectric cooling management.

title: Quantum Superfluid Vacuum Flow (QSVF): A Unified
summary: We present the complete Quantum Superfluid Vacuum Flow (QSVF) framework, a unified hydrodynamic formulation of fundamental physics that treats the vacuum of space as a single compressible, energetic Bose–Einstein Condensate (BEC) superfluid
content: We present the complete Quantum Superfluid Vacuum Flow (QSVF) framework, a unified hydrodynamic formulation of fundamental physics that treats the vacuum of space as a single compressible, energetic Bose–Einstein Condensate (BEC) superfluid of ambient density ρ₀ and background pressure P₀. Within this single physical substrate, elementary quarks, all three fermion generations, nuclear binding forces, electromagnetic radiation, weak decay, intrinsic inertial mass, emergent gravity, atomic orbitals, and stellar nucleosynthesis emerge as deterministic fluid-dynamic phenomena.Fractional quark charges (+2/3 and −1/3) are derived geometrically from full-sphere up-quark flux (+4πr²) and double-sided equatorial down-quark disk compression (−2πr²), while heavier quark flavors (s, c, b, t) and leptons (μ, τ, ν) arise as flux-invariant composite sink chains and excited standing-wave modes obeying 4π Madelung spinor closure (Sz = ±1/2 ħ). Strong nuclear confinement is derived from Mach-1 choked-flow Bernoulli suction (ρ_min = (2/3)ρ₀), with high-energy throat ruptures shedding spin-1 quantized vortex rings (three-jet collider events).Intrinsic rest mass is defined as the invariant QSVF mass consumption rate (m_b = τ₀ Ṁ_total), cleanly distinguishing invariant mass from relational weight (W = −m_b dv_rel/dt) and recovering the Painlevé–Gullstrand Schwarzschild metric via Unruh’s acoustic correspondence. Finally, we derive the QSVF Gamow stellar ignition temperature formula across Hydrogen, Helium-4, Carbon, Oxygen, and Silicon burning up to the Iron-56 polyhedral limit, demonstrate heavy-element synthesis via neutral [u + envelope] vacuum condensation, contrast QSVF against Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), and establish five falsifiable experimental tests.

title: Assessment and mapping of soil moisture at field capacity using machine learning methods in the Central Chernozem Belt of Russia
summary: Soil moisture at field capacity (SM FC ) is a key soil hydraulic property for assessing water-storage capacity, irrigation requirements, and crop-water availability, yet its regional distribution is difficult to characterize because it is c
content: Soil moisture at field capacity (SM FC ) is a key soil hydraulic property for assessing water-storage capacity, irrigation requirements, and crop-water availability, yet its regional distribution is difficult to characterize because it is controlled by interacting soil, climatic, topographic, and land-surface factors. To address the logistical constraints of direct regional matric potential measurements, this study applied an indirect, pedotransfer function (PTF)-augmented digital soil mapping framework to estimate and map SM FC at 0–30 cm depth and a matric potential of − 33 kPa across the Central Chernozem Belt of Russia using an explainable machine learning framework. A total of 2157 geo-referenced soil samples collected between 2023 and 2025 were combined with remote-sensing, terrain, climatic, geological, and spatial covariates defined within the SCORPAN framework. SM FC was estimated from van Genuchten water-retention parameters derived using pedotransfer functions, and three machine-learning algorithms, namely artificial neural network (ANN), support vector machine (SVM), and random forest (RF), were trained and independently evaluated using a 70:30 calibrations–validation design. The RF model provided the most accurate predictions in both datasets, achieving R 2 = 0.81, RMSE = 1.93, and PRD = 3.17 during calibration and R 2 = 0.89, RMSE = 1.45, and PRD = 3.25 during independent validation. ANN showed intermediate performance, whereas SVM produced the lowest accuracy. RF-based predictions revealed substantial and spatially heterogeneous variation in SM FC , with values ranging from 13.68 to 43.34, and no simple regional gradient. Variable-importance analysis identified NDVI, TWI, SAVI, and NDWI as the leading predictors, highlighting the relevance of vegetation condition and topographic moisture redistribution to the spatial pattern of soil water retention. Lower and upper prediction-limit maps further demonstrated that predictive uncertainty varied across the region. These findings indicate that explainable machine-learning methods, particularly RF, can support regional assessment of SM FC in environmentally heterogeneous agricultural systems, while uncertainty information remains necessary for cautious interpretation and responsible application in irrigation planning and soil–water management.

title: Carbon Cycle and the Biosphere
summary: Chapter 2 examines the carbon cycle and its connection to the biosphere, highlighting its significance in global climate change. It points out that various factors influence the carbon cycle, including human actions and natural events. The
content: Chapter 2 examines the carbon cycle and its connection to the biosphere, highlighting its significance in global climate change. It points out that various factors influence the carbon cycle, including human actions and natural events. The chapter explains the carbon cycle’s crucial role in the greenhouse effect and its impact on ocean ecosystems. It also looks at the behavior of atmospheric CO 2 , discussing historical, present, and future carbon emissions, along with the global carbon budget. The impact of climate change on the carbon cycle is analyzed, noting that various processes can complicate matters and that efforts to reduce carbon can have unexpected results. This chapter details the sources and sinks of CO 2 in the biosphere, including human-generated carbon. It outlines the elements of the global carbon cycle and the biosphere’s resources that contribute to it. The ocean carbon cycle is also discussed, portraying the ocean as a geosystem and explaining the carbon exchange between the atmosphere and the ocean. It covers the organic carbon cycle in various marine environments, such as upwellings and icy seas. Additionally, this chapter connects the carbon cycle to other biochemical cycles, including those of methane and nitrogen. It highlights peatlands as essential parts of the carbon cycle and their importance in climate change studies. Lastly, this chapter introduces new methods for removing CO 2 from the ocean, focusing on the potential use of renewable energy sources for this task.

title: Proton Dynamic Confluence Effect Enables Self‐Synchronized *H Source‐Storage‐Sink for Electrocatalytic Nitrate‐to‐Ammonia from Fertilizer Wastewater
summary: Fertilizer‐plant rinse wastewater is high‐concentration, low‐flow, sparsely distributed point‐source nitrate pollution, with nitrate‐nitrogen reaching thousands of ppm. Renewable‐energy‐driven electrochemical nitrate reduction (NO 3 RR) can
content: Fertilizer‐plant rinse wastewater is high‐concentration, low‐flow, sparsely distributed point‐source nitrate pollution, with nitrate‐nitrogen reaching thousands of ppm. Renewable‐energy‐driven electrochemical nitrate reduction (NO 3 RR) can convert nitrate into ammonia, but limited by flux imbalance between generation and consumption of active hydrogen (*H). Conventional catalysts cannot match *H supply and demand, causing hydrogen evolution or intermediate accumulation. We propose a Proton Dynamic Confluence Effect (PDCE) and design Co 2 P/Cu/LaPO 4 ternary heterojunction. Co 2 P supplies *H via water dissociation; surface PO 4 3 − on LaPO 4 acts as a dynamic proton buffer through reversible protonation (PO 4 3 − ⇌ HPO 4 2 − ); Cu is the consumption sink, activating nitrate and facilitating hydrogenation. This creates self‐synchronized source–storage–sink *H flux. In alkaline media, it achieves a maximum ammonia yield rate of 135.04 mg h − 1 cm − 2 and 94.9% Faradaic efficiency at −0.8 V vs. RHE. In situ spectroscopy captures reversible PO 4 3 − protonation and fast‐in–fast‐out intermediate kinetics; kinetic isotope and quenching experiments confirm a low‐free‐energy‐change PCET process. In real fertilizer‐plant wastewater (initial NO 3 − ‐N 3221 ppm) over 120 h operation, it achieves 99.85% nitrate removal, 35.15 g ammonia, and >90% Faradaic efficiency. PDCE shifts catalyst design from active‐site optimization to intermediate flux management, offering a universal strategy for electrocatalytic upgrading of fertilizer‐plant nitrate wastewater into ammonia.

title: GhDMP1b-D, a domain of unknown function 679 membrane Protein, coordinates carbon allocation to balance fiber and seed development in cotton
summary: Background Cotton is a vital global crop, chiefly valued for its natural fibers and seeds. The development of cotton fiber and seed is interconnected, with competition for carbon resources between the two. Domain of the Unknown Function 679
content: Background Cotton is a vital global crop, chiefly valued for its natural fibers and seeds. The development of cotton fiber and seed is interconnected, with competition for carbon resources between the two. Domain of the Unknown Function 679 (DUF679) membrane protein (DMP) is believed to play a crucial role in physiological processes such as reproductive development and senescence of plants. However, its function in the development of cotton fiber and seed remains unclear. In this study, genetic and functional analysis confirmed that GhDMP1b-D regulates cotton fiber and seed development. Results Ectopic expression of GhDMP1b-D in Arabidopsis facilitated root development but inhibited seed development. Knocking out GhDMP1b-D in cotton resulted in shorter fibers, thicker secondary cell walls, higher cellulose content, and larger seeds. RNA-seq analysis proposed that GhDMP1b-D might regulate the development of cotton fiber and seed by influencing the UDP-glucose synthesis pathway. Conclusions Collectively, our work unveils GhDMP1b-D as a novel genetic determinant in the carbon partitioning system that balances fiber and seed development in cotton, providing important insights into the metabolic regulation of sink strength in plants.

title: Data-Driven Ocean Emulation: Using Operator Inference to Emulate a Double Gyre Ocean System
summary: Ocean general circulation models are indispensable tools for climate research, yet their high computational cost limits many-query applications, including uncertainty quantification, large-ensemble forecasting, and scenario-based evaluation
content: Ocean general circulation models are indispensable tools for climate research, yet their high computational cost limits many-query applications, including uncertainty quantification, large-ensemble forecasting, and scenario-based evaluations of oceanic response to changing atmospheric forcing. Machine learning enables rapid emulation, but purely data-driven, “black-box” neural networks often lack interpretability and generalize poorly to unseen forcing conditions. In this work, we construct a physics-motivated, data-driven Operator Inference reduced-order model (OpInf ROM) capable of evolving the full threedimensional prognostic ocean state over decade-long simulation horizons. Applied to an idealized double-gyre basin driven by seasonally cycling wind and buoyancy forcing, the OpInf ROM combines learned quadratic dynamics with atmospheric forcing operators constructed from known surface forcing fields. To ensure physical consistency, linear constraints on the reduced operators enforce basin-integrated heat and salt budget closure. Evaluated on a wind-stress amplitude held out from training, the OpInf ROM accurately reproduces decadal-mean surface and interior states, the vertical thermohaline structure, and the scaling of gyre transport with forcing amplitude. The conservation constraints prevent spurious net heat and salt sources, ensuring internally consistent tracer budgets even when predicted tracer changes differ from the full-order model. Although the OpInf ROM progressively damps high-frequency mesoscale eddy variability, its computational speedup of over five orders of magnitude enables rapid evaluation of mean-state ocean sensitivity to variable atmospheric forcing. Plain Language Summary Numerical ocean models are vital for understanding how ocean currents transport heat and regulate global climate. However, their high computational cost makes it difficult to explore how oceans might respond to changing atmospheric conditions. Machine learning can speed up simulations, but purely data-driven models often fail when tested under new climate conditions. In this study, we developed a data-driven model that combines machine learning with known physical laws to simulate a decade of ocean circulation in a simplified ocean basin. We also enforce conservation of heat and salt, ensuring that changes in their total amounts are consistent with exchanges at the ocean surface. The model stays stable and accurately captures the average climate over ten years, though it gradually smooths out rapid, small-scale eddy features over time. Notably, it runs more than 100,000 times faster than a traditional ocean model and correctly predicts how ocean currents change under new wind patterns. This enables rapid exploration of “what-if” climate scenarios, making large-ensemble forecasting and uncertainty quantification computationally feasible.

title: Floating or Sinking Carbon Dioxide Clathrate Hydrate in Brines: Density Determination and Relevance to Seawater Desalination
summary: An experimental investigation was carried out to determine whether carbon dioxide clathrate hydrate, formed by reacting brines of various concentrations with carbon dioxide gas, floats or sinks in the remaining unreacted brine. This study a
content: An experimental investigation was carried out to determine whether carbon dioxide clathrate hydrate, formed by reacting brines of various concentrations with carbon dioxide gas, floats or sinks in the remaining unreacted brine. This study aims to advance clathrate hydrate-based seawater desalination and/or salt production. The carbon dioxide clathrate hydrate formed in the reactors is recovered together with the unreacted seawater as slurry and then sent to the solid–liquid separation process. Understanding whether the hydrate floats or sinks is essential for the design and operation of the process. In this study, floating or sinking was determined by visual inspection when the system reached three-phase equilibrium among sodium chloride aqueous solution, carbon dioxide clathrate hydrate, and carbon dioxide gas. The equilibrium sodium chloride mass fraction in the brine ranged from 0.095 to 0.150. At higher mass fraction, the carbon dioxide clathrate hydrate floated in the aqueous solution. The critical mass fraction, defined as the average of the two mass fractions bounding the transition from sinking to floating, increased with pressure and was 0.109 ± 0.011 at approximately 1 MPa and 0.118 ± 0.007 at approximately 2 MPa. The corresponding equilibrium temperatures were approximately 266 and 272 K, respectively. Because sinking and floating correspond to opposite relative density orderings of the clathrate hydrate and the aqueous solution, the density of clathrate hydrate was determined from the density of aqueous solution at the corresponding intermediate condition to be 1092 ± 9 kg/m3 at about 1 MPa and 1105 ± 7 kg/m3 at about 2 MPa, suggesting that the hydrate density increases with increasing pressure. These density data were compared with values reported in previous studies based on physical characterization. Finally, the relevance of these findings to seawater desalination technology was discussed.

title: Integrating optical and microwave satellite observations improves aboveground biomass estimation across Arctic-Boreal Northwestern North America
summary: Accelerated warming of the Arctic greatly impacts vegetation dynamics and biogeochemical cycles. Enhanced large-scale monitoring of aboveground biomass (AGB) is needed to improve understanding of biosphere responses to warming. While optica
content: Accelerated warming of the Arctic greatly impacts vegetation dynamics and biogeochemical cycles. Enhanced large-scale monitoring of aboveground biomass (AGB) is needed to improve understanding of biosphere responses to warming. While optical remote sensing can infer AGB from photosynthetic productivity observed at the canopy surface, Vegetation Optical Depth (VOD), the degree of attenuation of microwave energy through vertical structure of vegetation, is directly sensitive to bulk AGB. We use multiple linear regression (MLR) to integrate multiple optical vegetation indices (VIs) from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and VOD frequencies from the Vegetation Optical Depth Climate Archive (VODCA) to produce an improved annual AGB product, named here AGBVM, over Alaska and Northern Canada for years 2003-2017 and for forest, shrub, grass, crop, and tundra vegetation cover classes. AGBVM was spatially calibrated (2017) and evaluated (2010) using the European Space Agency’s Climate Change Initiative gridded AGB product as the reference dataset. Our model integrating C-band VOD, visible atmospherically resistant index (VARI) and near infrared reflectance of vegetation (Nirvi) was the best predictor of AGB. R2 values are 0.55 and 0.64 and RMSE values are 26 and 23 Mg ha-1 (2017 calibration and 2010 validation years, respectively). AGBVM demonstrated the highest degree of sensitivity to pre- and post-fire mean AGB anomalies relative to other gridded products. AGBVM presents a novel dataset with improved capacity for capturing spatiotemporal AGB variability across Arctic-Boreal northwestern North America, with wide applications in carbon stock monitoring and disturbance detection in high-latitude vegetation communities. This approach utilizes globally available datasets and can be expanded to estimate AGB across arctic and boreal regions of the northern hemisphere.

title: Coastal ocean properties in the Galápagos upwelling region
summary: The Galapagos Islands and the Galapagos Cold Pool to their west serve as a biological hotspot due to frequent episodic upwelling of subsurface waters high in nutrients. The region’s primary productivity provides an important base to multipl
content: The Galapagos Islands and the Galapagos Cold Pool to their west serve as a biological hotspot due to frequent episodic upwelling of subsurface waters high in nutrients. The region’s primary productivity provides an important base to multiple endemic species within the ecosystem as well as a sink for the anomalously high sea surface pCO2 that also results from the upwelling. In situ observations of near-surface seawater properties collected between the cold pool and the coast of the archipelago are limited, despite interest in the region’s distinctive biological and physical processes. Here we describe a unique and comprehensive dataset from the region spanning physical and biogeochemical observations. We identify cold, saline waters that are predominantly oversaturated in pCO2 relative to the atmosphere, suggesting upwelling. Near-surface currents tend not to be aligned with concurrent wind measurements and profiles of upper-ocean currents show substantial variability in both time and space, and a strong westward current south of the archipelago. These coastal observations serve as a complement to previous studies of the broader, offshore region describing the cold pool. Unlike further offshore, we see little sign of the eastward Equatorial Under Current, suggesting that it is steered around the Galapagos before reaching the near-shore locations observed in this study. These findings provide a novel record of near-shore ocean properties in an important equatorial region with limited observations, which can serve as a dry season baseline for future studies to quantify seasonal to long-term regional changes.

title: Long-term responses of sediment nitrogen cycling to environmental change in a semi-enclosed inland sea
summary: Sediment nitrogen cycling regulates nutrient retention, ecosystem functioning, and greenhouse gas emissions in coastal seas. However, its response to long-term environmental change and the underlying drivers remain poorly understood because
content: Sediment nitrogen cycling regulates nutrient retention, ecosystem functioning, and greenhouse gas emissions in coastal seas. However, its response to long-term environmental change and the underlying drivers remain poorly understood because of limited long-term observations. Using Harima Nada as a study system, we combined multi-decadal monitoring data with a one-dimensional sediment model to reconstruct sediment nitrogen cycling and sediment–water nitrogen fluxes from 1992 to 2021. We show that interannual variations in sediment nitrogen cycling are driven by changes in organic matter deposition, its degradability, microphytobenthos activity, and oxygen-dependent nitrogen transformations. Attribution experiments further reveal that eutrophication recovery substantially alters sediment nitrogen cycling by reducing particulate organic nitrogen inputs, whereas nitrogen accumulated during eutrophic periods is gradually recycled to the overlying water as benthic dissolved inorganic nitrogen fluxes. Consequently, the magnitude and persistence of sediment nutrient legacy effects are determined by the intensity and duration of eutrophication. In contrast, seawater warming exerts only negligible effects on sediment nitrogen cycling over decadal timescales. These findings establish a process-based attribution framework for evaluating the impacts of long-term sediment nitrogen dynamics, identifying eutrophication rather than seawater warming as the dominant driver and highlighting the importance of sediment legacy effects for coastal nutrient management.

title: An intercomparison of modern GOSAT XCO 2 data products
summary: Space-based observations of column-mean dry-air mole fraction of carbon dioxide (XCO2) from multiple satellites such as GOSAT, GOSAT-2, OCO-2, and OCO-3 are often used to infer global and regional-scale carbon fluxes. Several algorithms hav
content: Space-based observations of column-mean dry-air mole fraction of carbon dioxide (XCO2) from multiple satellites such as GOSAT, GOSAT-2, OCO-2, and OCO-3 are often used to infer global and regional-scale carbon fluxes. Several algorithms have been developed to retrieve XCO2 from these measurements, and they make different choices regarding the retrieval itself, pre- and post-filtering, and post-retrieval bias correction. These choices can yield differences in sounding-matched XCO2 as well as in the location and density of quality-filtered soundings. Both of these traits, actual XCO2 as well as good sounding spatiotemporal distributions, can lead to differences in inferred carbon fluxes. In this work, we present an extensive intercomparison of XCO2 from six retrieval algorithms operating on data from the GOSAT satellite, over the period 2010–2022. The retrieval algorithms include the FOCAL v4 algorithm, the University of Leicester v7.3 algorithm, the NIES v3.05 algorithm, the JAXA EORC v3 algorithm, the RemoTeC v2.4.1 algorithm, and the ACOS v11 algorithm. These algorithms differ in terms of sounding selection, CO2 and meteorological priors, molecular spectroscopy, assumptions regarding cloud and aerosol scattering, and post-retrieval filtering and bias correction. For each XCO2 product, we evaluate throughput, accuracy, temporal stability, and robustness of their posterior uncertainty estimate. These metrics are obtained from comparisons with co-located Total Carbon Column Observing Network (TCCON, GGG2020) data and with XCO2 from a suite of carbon inverse models. The models discriminate among the products more effectively than TCCON because of their superior global coverage. We find that the six products differ significantly in terms of all these metrics, though it is often difficult to identify the cause of the differences (e.g. forward model, filtering, and bias correction) without further research. These large discrepancies suggest that poorer-performing algorithms should be examined with scrutiny, with the hope that all such algorithms can be improved, to maximally leverage observations from both present and future XCO2-sensitive satellites in informing the global carbon cycle.

title: Hierarchically Bridged Graphite Foam/Cellulose Aerogel Phase Change Composites Reconciling High Thermal Conductivity and Latent Heat
summary: Phase change composites (PCCs) are promising for thermal management and solar thermal storage, yet reconciling high thermal conductivity with high latent heat remains challenging. Thermally conductive scaffolds accelerate heat transfer but
content: Phase change composites (PCCs) are promising for thermal management and solar thermal storage, yet reconciling high thermal conductivity with high latent heat remains challenging. Thermally conductive scaffolds accelerate heat transfer but dilute the phase‐change component and disturb crystallization, whereas polymeric porous supports provide structural confinement but suffer from sluggish thermal transport. Herein, a hierarchical composite is constructed by forming a crosslinked hydroxyethyl cellulose‐polyethylene glycol (PEG) network within mesophase pitch‐based graphite foam (MPGF), followed by vacuum impregnation of the scaffold with PEG. The continuous MPGF provides a primary heat transfer pathway and mechanical reinforcement, while the directional cellulose network bridges and subdivides MPGF macropores into a secondary porous scaffold. The PEG segments in the cellulose network not only improve interfacial compatibility with the impregnated PEG but also guide its crystallization within the refined pores. Therefore, the composite exhibits a thermal conductivity of 53.41 W m −1 K −1 and a latent enthalpy of 196.83 J g −1 . Benefiting from rapid heat spreading and sustained thermal release, it achieves efficient solar‐thermal storage and delivers a thermoelectric voltage of 391.5 mV at 200 mW cm −2 . This hierarchical architecture offers an effective strategy for integrating rapid heat transfer, efficient latent‐heat utilization, and solar thermoelectric conversion in PCCs.

title: A kinetic model of polyamine metabolism identifies spermine oxidase as a driver of the senescence-associated polyamine shift
summary: Polyamines, namely putrescine, spermidine and spermine, are essential polycations. Their homeostasis is governed by a nonlinear network of biosynthesis, catabolism, transport, and feedback control. We present an 18-variable ordinary differe
content: Polyamines, namely putrescine, spermidine and spermine, are essential polycations. Their homeostasis is governed by a nonlinear network of biosynthesis, catabolism, transport, and feedback control. We present an 18-variable ordinary differential equation model of intracellular polyamine metabolism that couples biosynthesis, acetylation and oxidation catabolism, antizyme feedback, ornithine decarboxylase dimerization, polyamine-dependent ribosomal frameshifting, reversible DNA and RNA binding, and spermine oxidase (SMOX)-driven acrolein production. A single literature-based parameter set reproduces the polyamine profiles of proliferating and senescent HepG2 cells within experimental error, including inversion of the spermine-to-spermidine ratio from 3.09 to 0.61. This inversion arises not from contracted biosynthesis but from SMOX induction, which oxidizes spermine directly to spermidine while biosynthetic throughput is maintained. SMOX becomes the majority route of spermine catabolism and raises the steady-state acrolein burden $$\approx$$ 3.8-fold. An ensemble of independent fits shows that this attribution and the predicted effect of SMOX inhibition hold for every parameter set that reproduces the measured pools. The model predicts that selective SMOX inhibition lowers acrolein and reverses the ratio inversion together.

title: Differential and bin-integrated power-law particle size distribution (PSD) and biomass size spectra (BSS) formulations
summary: The particle size distribution (PSD) and biomass size spectra (BSS) are key properties of ecosystems that are often described or modeled using a power law. The slope of this power law conveys key information such as ecosystem energy transfe
content: The particle size distribution (PSD) and biomass size spectra (BSS) are key properties of ecosystems that are often described or modeled using a power law. The slope of this power law conveys key information such as ecosystem energy transfer efficiency and the resultant bulk optical properties of a particle assemblage. The choice of size metric and concentration unit used to describe the PSD or BSS, and choices of binning scheme and bin integration as opposed to normalization by bin width (i.e., a differential or density function form) influence the resultant power-law slope for one and the same physical PSD. This makes it harder to compare various slopes in the literature and in models and data sets. Here I provide a systematic review of PSD formulations and their relationships, with mathematical proofs, focusing on the resultant relationships among equivalent power-law slopes for differential and bin-integrated PSDs of assumed spherical particles/cells of constant density. The central part of this contribution is a summary reference table of these slope relationships. In addition, scientific code is provided that illustrates the various PSD formulations and slope relationships. Both research and pedagogical uses of this work are envisioned.

title: Chemical reactivity assessment of sediment organic matter: Comparison with thermal methods
summary: Continental shelf sediments are important blue carbon habitats, but they are also exposed to anthropogenic disturbances such as bottom trawling, which increase oxygen exposure and thereby enhance organic carbon remineralisation. Understandi
content: Continental shelf sediments are important blue carbon habitats, but they are also exposed to anthropogenic disturbances such as bottom trawling, which increase oxygen exposure and thereby enhance organic carbon remineralisation. Understanding the susceptibility of shelf sedimentary organic matter to oxidation is therefore important, and research has moved beyond simple estimates of total carbon stocks towards characterising the potential vulnerability of this stored organic carbon. Here, we employ a modified chemical oxidation approach (acid-dichromate) to assess organic carbon reactivity in muddy shelf sediments from the Fladen Ground in the North Sea and compare it with the prevalent thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) technique. Sediments were oxidised with acidified dichromate at 5 °C for 1.5 to 24 hours, and the fractional loss of organic carbon was quantified. Maximum (~30 %) of the chemically oxidisable organic carbon was lost during the first three hours of treatment, with only a limited additional loss over longer oxidation times. The fractional carbon loss after three hours showed a strong positive relationship (r = 0.69) with the thermally labile organic matter determined by TGA.
