title: Brewed with Balance: Expanding the Lacey Act to Combat Global Deforestation from Coffee Bean Farming
summary: Coffee has become a staple in the average American's life. Today, coffee symbolizes energy, productivity, and creativity, with nearly three in four Americans drinking it daily. However, it is unlikely that the average American pauses to thi
content: Coffee has become a staple in the average American's life. Today, coffee symbolizes energy, productivity, and creativity, with nearly three in four Americans drinking it daily. However, it is unlikely that the average American pauses to think about how their morning coffee is produced, nor is it likely that they reflect on the environmental impact that is required to harvest their daily brew. Many Americans are thus unaware that the combination of high coffee demand, modern farming practices, and climate change is threatening forests and biodiversity.

title: Going 'Rogue': Supreme Court 'Major Questions Doctrine' — Preempting Power over Power
summary: Legal power over power. A controversial 1,300-page administrative agency order about United States (“U.S.”) power in the final months of President Biden’s administration traversed the Supreme Court’s often proclaimed “bright line” barricade
content: Legal power over power. A controversial 1,300-page administrative agency order about United States (“U.S.”) power in the final months of President Biden’s administration traversed the Supreme Court’s often proclaimed “bright line” barricade restricting Presidential power. This traversal escalated into a “Major Questions Doctrine” legal clash over the separation of powers. Multiple states immediately challenged this administrative order after the future-Chair of the issuing Executive Branch agency stated that his agency deliberately and knowingly chose to violate the U.S. Constitution.

title: Greenwashing Causes Beef Between Protein Companies, Consumers, and the Food, Safety and Inspection Service: The Need for Environment-Related Food Labeling Regulations
summary: Tyson Foods Inc. (“Tyson”), a corporation that produces around 20 percent of the meat sold in the United States (“U.S.”), has been claiming since 2021 that it will reach net zero emissions by 2050. If successful, this objective would result
content: Tyson Foods Inc. (“Tyson”), a corporation that produces around 20 percent of the meat sold in the United States (“U.S.”), has been claiming since 2021 that it will reach net zero emissions by 2050. If successful, this objective would result in the popular food company cutting carbon emissions so drastically that the residual carbon emitted could be stored by nature, leaving zero carbon in the atmosphere. To help accomplish this daring goal, Tyson announced the Climate Smart Beef Program to tackle emissions from “pasture to production” or, in other terms, from cradle-to-gate. Cradle-to-gate is a Life Cycle Assessment (“LCA”) used to measure the environmental footprint a product leaves from the time it is extracted (the cradle) to the time it leaves the factory doors (the gate). The Climate Smart Beef Program advertised Tyson’s commitment to a 30 percent reduction in its cradle-to-gate greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, implying massive reductions in each stage of the agricultural and retail processes.

title: Consumer Protection in Cyberspace
source: tripleC Communication Capitalism & Critique Open Access Journal for a Global Sustainable Information Society
summary: This critical essay introduces the problem of discrimination enabled through the use of transaction-generated-information derived from the analysis of user behaviors within the network environment. The essay begins by describing how segment
content: This critical essay introduces the problem of discrimination enabled through the use of transaction-generated-information derived from the analysis of user behaviors within the network environment. The essay begins by describing how segments of the population that are already vulnerable become further victimized through the strategic use of discriminatory algorithms in support of identification, classification, segmentation, and targeting. In response, it evaluates a set of policy options that might be used to limit the harm and compensate the victims of these inherently dangerous technologies. Traditional approaches that stress the protection of privacy through restrictions on the collection and use of personal information are compared with alternatives based on individual and class actions under tort law, as well as more traditional regulatory approaches developed in the area of consumer products safety and environmental regulation.

title: Exploring the distributional implications of targeted residential electrification in California
summary: The economics of residential electrification in high-cost electricity regions remain uncertain. Using metered data from over 20,000 California homes, we assess the economic, environmental, and equity impacts of end-use electrification under
content: The economics of residential electrification in high-cost electricity regions remain uncertain. Using metered data from over 20,000 California homes, we assess the economic, environmental, and equity impacts of end-use electrification under rollout strategies based on household income and gas infrastructure age. Even under favorable electricity rates, only 15% of households achieve positive net present values (NPVs). Cost-effectiveness improves with deeper electrification scenarios, particularly when more costs are shifted to fixed charges and for homes with existing air conditioning—54–67% of these households break even when electrifying space heating, compared to fewer than 5% of those without. Income-based rebates more than double the share of low- and moderate-income households with positive NPVs. Prioritizing areas with aging gas infrastructure yields emissions reductions on par with high-income-led adoption and avoids costly pipeline replacement, but requires the highest subsidy to achieve cost-effectiveness across all households. These findings highlight trade-offs in designing equitable electrification strategies.

title: Impacts of medications for obesity on global health and the environment
summary: A new generation of medications for obesity could transform the global food system. While research has explored their health impacts, their implications for global food demand and land use remain unquantified. We apply a global food system
content: A new generation of medications for obesity could transform the global food system. While research has explored their health impacts, their implications for global food demand and land use remain unquantified. We apply a global food system model to project the impact of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1) uptake to 2050 among people with obesity under two scenarios: reduced calorie intake while maintaining dietary composition, and reduced calorie intake combined with shifts towards the EAT-Lancet diet. Compared with the Reference scenario, GLP-1-mediated calorie reduction alone results in up to 6.6 million avoided deaths globally in 2050 and 32 Mha more natural land area, reflecting reductions in cropland, pasture and managed forest. Combining GLP-1 use with EAT-Lancet dietary shifts increases these estimates to 7.7 million avoided deaths and 46 Mha more natural land. Lower food prices increase food consumption among untreated populations, including unhealthy foods, partially offsetting these gains.

title: Governing cryospheric risk beyond political timeframes
summary: Cryospheric risks unfold over decades to millennia, while climate governance remains tied to short political cycles. We argue that cryosphere science must be embedded in governance mechanisms that connect near-term decisions with long-term
content: Cryospheric risks unfold over decades to millennia, while climate governance remains tied to short political cycles. We argue that cryosphere science must be embedded in governance mechanisms that connect near-term decisions with long-term accountability for irreversible change.

title: Convergence in access to clean cooking fuels across selected African economies: implications for health and environmental sustainability
summary: This study investigates convergence in access to clean cooking fuels across twelve African economies over the period 2000–2022, applying Phillips and Sul’s (2007) club convergence framework to World Bank World Development Indicators data. I
content: This study investigates convergence in access to clean cooking fuels across twelve African economies over the period 2000–2022, applying Phillips and Sul’s (2007) club convergence framework to World Bank World Development Indicators data. In this framework, the null hypothesis of convergence is not rejected when the log-t test’s t-statistic exceeds the critical value of −1.65; the reported t-statistic of 7.7429 substantially exceeds this threshold, confirming full-panel convergence across all twelve economies in the long run, albeit at varying speeds. Trend plots and heat maps reveal persistent regional disparities, with high-access countries concentrated in Northern and Southern Africa and low-access laggards in Central and East Africa, and robustness checks across alternative time periods show that this convergence is not uniform over time, with progress remaining fragile and contingent on sustained policy effort. Drawing on the established literature rather than on analysis conducted in this study, the observed patterns carry plausible implications for public health, through reduced indoor air pollution and associated respiratory and cardiovascular disease, and for environmental sustainability, through reduced deforestation and lower greenhouse gas emissions. The findings point to the importance of differentiated, country-specific strategies for achieving Sustainable Development Goal 7 while advancing public health and environmental resilience in Africa.

title: An integrated fuzzy framework for selecting optimal emerging energy storage systems for grid applications: A stakeholder-driven approach
summary: The sustainability-driven emphasis on advancing Energy Storage Technologies (EST) has empowered decision-makers to enhance power grid resilience and promote smart grid development. These grids incorporate various technologies, including EST
content: The sustainability-driven emphasis on advancing Energy Storage Technologies (EST) has empowered decision-makers to enhance power grid resilience and promote smart grid development. These grids incorporate various technologies, including EST, Artificial Intelligence, and the Internet of Things, all of which interact constructively to enhance grid efficiency and resilience. Selecting the appropriate EST, however, is a complex challenge due to the diversity of available options, varied selection criteria, and the involvement of multiple stakeholders with unique interests. This study proposes an integrated Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) framework, informed by stakeholder analysis, to systematically evaluate emerging EST across multiple dimensions. A pairwise comparison was conducted by a group of experts using linguistic terms to assess decision criteria and sub-criteria. SF-AHP ensured consistent judgments among the decision-makers (CR < 0.10). TOPSIS ranked HES first, followed by LAES, A−CAES, GES, Ni−Zn, VRFB, SIB, and SSB. To validate the ranking results, we employed the PIV, EDAS, CODAS, MOORA, VIKOR, and ALWAS methods to mitigate the limitations of MCDM techniques. The finding that HES ranks first in six of seven methods shows that the result is conditional on the selected data, criteria, weights, and system boundaries. Sensitivity analysis indicated that HES is the most robust option and the most sensitive to Energy Density. A-CAES and LAES showed potential to outperform HES when placing greater weight on HES's weakness criteria. The results generally highlight the promising potential of HES for sustainable energy solutions in grid applications compared to other ESTs.

title: Spatial interference in policy evaluation. A causal framework for CAP organic farming support
summary: This paper investigates the identification and estimation of policy impacts in the presence of spatial interference, an aspect often overlooked in treatment-effect studies. In many policy contexts, spatial interference arises as economic an
content: This paper investigates the identification and estimation of policy impacts in the presence of spatial interference, an aspect often overlooked in treatment-effect studies. In many policy contexts, spatial interference arises as economic and behavioural interactions among neighbouring agents influence both treatment assignment and outcomes. Focusing on agri-environmental policies, we develop a conceptual framework for farmers’ decision-making that explicitly incorporates spatial interference. We apply alternative spatial econometric approaches to evaluate the impact of the European Union’s support for organic farming, using data from the Italian Farm Accountancy Data Network (FADN) for the period 2008–2020. We find that organic support has, on average, a positive effect on farm income, and that accounting for spatial interactions enriches the interpretation of this effect by distinguishing own-treatment impacts from local exposure mechanisms. Among the methods considered, spatially explicit propensity-score matching approaches provide the most robust and interpretable estimates, although they remain sensitive to unobserved confounding and misspecification of the observed neighborhood structure. Parametric methods appear more robust to spatial gaps, but their spatial autoregressive variants still appear vulnerable to network misspecification.

title: Methane outburst driven by magma–sediment interactions at Fentale Volcano detected by satellite
summary: Magmatic intrusions into sedimentary rocks can release carbon-based greenhouse gases, dominantly methane, and have been linked to rapid changes in past climate. However, modern volcanic systems typically emit very little methane, meaning th
content: Magmatic intrusions into sedimentary rocks can release carbon-based greenhouse gases, dominantly methane, and have been linked to rapid changes in past climate. However, modern volcanic systems typically emit very little methane, meaning that appropriate analogues are lacking. Here we report satellite measurements of an outburst of methane and carbon dioxide from a restless but non-erupting volcano in the East African Rift. Following a mega-dyke intrusion in 2025, Fentale Volcano (Ethiopia) released at least 38.2 ± 3.9 kt CH 4 over 3 months and at least 2.9 ± 1.0 MtCO 2 . The peak methane emission rate of 157 ± 41 t h −1 is comparable to major industrial blowouts and approximately four orders of magnitude higher than methane emission rates from other volcanic systems. The emissions coincided with localized ground subsidence and thermal anomalies within Fentale’s caldera. We propose that the intrusion disrupted an impermeable cap beneath which methane, derived from hydrocarbon-rich sediments, was trapped. This single outburst is small compared with annual emissions from natural and anthropogenic sources, but demonstrates an unrecognized source of episodic methane emissions, providing insight into greenhouse gas release from magmatic–sedimentary systems.

title: Trace‐Metal‐Assisted Flash Synthesis for Fast‐Charging Graphite Anodes
summary: Graphite has remained the dominant anode material in lithium–ion batteries (LIBs), powering portable electronics and electric vehicles (EVs). However, sluggish Li + diffusion kinetics in natural and synthetic graphite can severely limit cha
content: Graphite has remained the dominant anode material in lithium–ion batteries (LIBs), powering portable electronics and electric vehicles (EVs). However, sluggish Li + diffusion kinetics in natural and synthetic graphite can severely limit charging rates. Overcoming this bottleneck requires the rational design of graphite architectures that enable rapid Li + transport in LIBs. Here, we disclose a trace‐metal‐assisted flash (TMF) process for the millisecond synthesis of catalytic flashed graphite (CFGr) with exceptionally fast‐charging capabilities. The TMF process induces in situ formation of trace nickel nanoclusters that catalyze ultrafast graphitization of amorphous carbon into highly ordered graphite within <1 s. Raman spectroscopy shows an exceedingly clean graphite material with I D / I G of 0.09, with calculations yielding an interlayer bonding energy ( E b ) of −2.297 eV, while diffraction reveals an interlayer spacing (d 002 ) of 3.4 Å. These features enhance structural stability and Li + accessibility. Consequently, optimized CFGr achieves a high reversible capacity of 347.4 mAh g −1 at 0.25 C and retains 158.8 mAh g −1 at 15 C with 80% capacity retention after 1000 cycles, outperforming the rate and cyclability of both commercial graphite and graphite prepared by flash Joule heating. The TMF route can replace conventional energy‐intensive graphitization, reducing energy use and emissions by over 80% and lowering the production cost of premium fast‐charging synthetic graphite by ∼80% to only US$0.84 kg −1 . These findings establish a promising pathway to advance fast‐charging graphite anodes into next‐generation LIBs.

title: Sustainably producing green fuel ammonia in equatorial waters and piping it worldwide, and removing atmospheric CO2 to return to the 1960s temperature rise level by 2100
summary: Global warming poses a serious threat to humanity and ecosystems, yet a fundamental solution has not yet been found. This study proposes a strategy to overcome the challenges currently facing solar and wind power generation, such as limited
content: Global warming poses a serious threat to humanity and ecosystems, yet a fundamental solution has not yet been found. This study proposes a strategy to overcome the challenges currently facing solar and wind power generation, such as limited installation space, reduced grid inertia, and the difficulty of large-scale energy storage. It involves the decentralized deployment of numerous floating offshore photovoltaic (FOPV) plants across the vast equatorial waters. Green hydrogen is produced using electricity generated by FOPV, and green fuel ammonia—a carbon-free energy—is synthesized. This enables global-scale transportation and storage via pipeline networks, minimizing energy transmission losses. Furthermore, by removing CO2eq from the atmosphere, global temperature rise will be returned to 1960s levels by 2100. Numerical analyses of four scenarios for global warming from 1850 to 2100 revealed that early implementation would reduce the cost of returning global temperature rise to 1960s levels and mitigate health impacts. With no fuel costs, economies of scale, and artificial intelligence (AI)- equipped robots, electricity costs—including CO2eq removal—could fall below current levels. In addition, vehicles equipped with hydrogen-added ammonia internal combustion engines could replace conventional gasoline-powered, and electric vehicle vehicles. It also becomes possible to synthesize green naphtha using CO2 captured from the atmosphere and green hydrogen, enabling low-cost supply. Although the strategies proposed in this study require validation testing prior to practical implementation, they hold the potential to lead to effective energy policies with global impact that can facilitate transitions to sustainable green energy spanning the lifetime of the Sun.

title: Potassium Management under Different Crop Establishment Methods for Improving the Productivity of the Rice (Oryza sativa L.)—Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) Cropping System: A Review
source: Journal of Global Innovations in Agricultural Sciences
summary: A population of over 150 million in South Asia, particularly in the Indo-Gangetic Plains, relies on the rice-wheat cropping system (RWCS) as the source of their food and means of livelihood. Despite being a necessity of the Green Revolution
content: A population of over 150 million in South Asia, particularly in the Indo-Gangetic Plains, relies on the rice-wheat cropping system (RWCS) as the source of their food and means of livelihood. Despite being a necessity of the Green Revolution, problems such as yield stagnation, soil erosion, groundwater depletion, and burning residue pollution are currently straining its long-term sustainability. Traditional practices like puddled transplanted rice followed by conventionally tilled wheat have further strained soil health and increased resource use. Potassium (K), the third most important nutrient after nitrogen and phosphorus, is vital for maintaining crop productivity, yet its use in India remains low. Continuous high crop uptake without adequate replenishment has led to a negative K balance, depleting soil fertility over time. To address this, resource-conserving technologies—such as zero tillage, direct-seeded rice, mechanical transplanting, and crop residue recycling—combined with potassium management can play a key role in restoring soil nutrient pools. Moreover, adopting alternative sources like potassium-solubilizing bacteria and organic amendments (vermicompost, crop residues) can improve potassium availability while reducing dependence on costly imported fertilizers. Integrated potassium management across different crop establishment methods not only improves soil properties but also ensures sustainable productivity and profitability of the RWCS. By embracing these practices, farmers can overcome stagnating yields, preserve soil health, and reduce environmental risks, thereby strengthening the resilience and future of this vital cropping system in South Asia. Keywords: Cropping system, economics, food security, soil health, groundwater, zero tillage, crop residue, insect and pest resistance, potassium management.

title: Sustainable port-city connectivity using remote gates and battery-electric truck operations
source: Transportation Research Part D Transport and Environment
summary: Growing maritime trade has intensified congestion and environmental pressures in port cities. Existing approaches primarily focus on port efficiency or promote alternative freight transport modes; however, road transport remains dominant, r
content: Growing maritime trade has intensified congestion and environmental pressures in port cities. Existing approaches primarily focus on port efficiency or promote alternative freight transport modes; however, road transport remains dominant, resulting in persistent congestion and emissions on port-access-road. This study proposes a network-oriented strategy combining a chassis-based remote gate (CRG) at the urban periphery with battery-electric trucks (BET) for low-emission port-CRG transport. A comparative framework is developed to assess the alignment and misalignment of port-handling capacity and hinterland connectivity under coordinated and port-centric governance settings. Using discrete-event simulation for a UK port case, the CRG-BET framework is compared with a conventional system in terms of cost, emissions, congestion, and traffic density. Results highlight the importance of aligning port and hinterland handling capacities and demonstrate the efficiency of the CRG-BET strategy in reducing system costs under port and hinterland-connectivity constraints, cutting emissions and easing congestion, thereby supporting more sustainable port-hinterland logistics.

title: A ‘rights-based’ approach to climate change and biodiversity loss: rights of humans, Nature and future generations
source: Ethics in Science and Environmental Politics
summary: Climate change and biodiversity loss, as well as their responses, including mitigation, adaptation and conservation measures, have human rights implications. An analysis of the linkages between human rights, biodiversity and climate change
content: Climate change and biodiversity loss, as well as their responses, including mitigation, adaptation and conservation measures, have human rights implications. An analysis of the linkages between human rights, biodiversity and climate change can support the design of co-beneficial actions and policies conjointly tackling issues at the intersection of biodiversity, climate change and human rights. This paper identifies the implications of climate change and biodiversity loss for human rights and vice versa in order to offer a comprehensive conceptualization of the human rights-biodiversity-climate change linkages. One of the strengths of a rights-based approach lies in how it highlights the perspectives of climate and biodiversity loss victims. The limitations of the rights-based approach can be complemented by other legal or social strategies. This paper offers an overview of specific established rights of humans, Nature and future generations, and their linkages (co-beneficial, co-detrimental and trade-offs) to climate change and biodiversity (e.g. in terms of human rights violations). Finally, 3 key pathways for stakeholders are identified: (1) prioritize synergies and take a transdisciplinary approach to trade-offs between different rights and climate and biodiversity issues; (2) diversify litigation and communication strategies (e.g. story-telling); and (3) strengthen emerging rights and tools such as the human right to a healthy environment.

title: Porous carbon-based materials for electrochemical CO 2 capture by supercapacitive swing adsorption
summary: Electrochemical supercapacitive swing adsorption (SSA) is an emerging low-energy CO2 capture technology that couples reversible charge storage with electrically driven CO2 uptake and release. Porous carbon electrodes are central to SSA beca
content: Electrochemical supercapacitive swing adsorption (SSA) is an emerging low-energy CO2 capture technology that couples reversible charge storage with electrically driven CO2 uptake and release. Porous carbon electrodes are central to SSA because they govern charge storage, ion adsorption and transport, and interfacial CO2 enrichment, thereby determining capture performance. However, the relationships between carbon structure, interfacial electrochemistry, and CO2 capture mechanisms remain poorly understood. This review provides a carbon-centered perspective on SSA. First, the fundamentals of SSA, including cell configurations, electrode materials, and proposed capture mechanisms, are summarized, with particular attention to the evolution of carbon electrodes from commercial porous carbons to tailored porous carbons, quinone-functionalized carbons, and covalent organic framework-based composites. Then, emerging structure–performance relationships and derived empirical design principles for SSA electrodes are discussed, focusing on the influence of surface area, pore architecture, and surface chemistry on CO2 capture capacity, kinetics, and energy consumption. Finally, key challenges and opportunities in mechanistic understanding, material and device design, evaluation under realistic conditions, integration of CO2 capture with utilization, and technoeconomic analysis and life-cycle assessment are highlighted. By linking carbon structure to interfacial processes and device-level performance, this review provides a framework for the rational design of scalable SSA systems for electrochemical carbon capture.

title: REFRAMING WASTE AT ABURI COMMUNITY, GHANA: ART AS A RESPONSE TO URBAN CONSUMERISM
summary: This creative, art-based study, underpinned by a phenomenological design, employs a pragmatic approach to propose an alternative solution to solid waste and the associated pollution. In this contemporary era characterised by urbanisation, i
content: This creative, art-based study, underpinned by a phenomenological design, employs a pragmatic approach to propose an alternative solution to solid waste and the associated pollution. In this contemporary era characterised by urbanisation, industrialisation, and high consumerism, waste generation cannot be overlooked as a critical issue in the global sustainability discourse. This interventionist study investigates the socio-economic and ecological impacts of dominant solid waste materials in the Aburi community, with particular attention to the effects of inadequate management strategies. In this context, four interconnected investigative concerns were addressed by integrating sustainability ideals and aesthetic principles, thereby unifying theoretical and practical dimensions. This qualitative research, underpinned by Behavioural Change, Transformative Learning, and Eco-aesthetic theories, examined the perspectives of purposefully recruited participants using purposive and snowball sampling techniques. Data were generated through personal interviews and focus group discussions, while both participant and non-participant observations were employed to elicit insights beyond verbal interpretations across the study’s phases. The conclusions drawn from the various chronological phases of the study, including interpretations from the participants, perspectives, and the researchers’ observations, underscore the study’s potential to foster the recontextualisation of waste for aesthetic and sustainability significance.

title: Can litigation protect the health and wellbeing of Indigenous Peoples and Traditional Country from climate change impacts? A case study applying the Native Title Act 1993 in Australia
source: Journal of Southern Hemisphere Earth System Science
summary: Indigenous Peoples have stewardship of their physical environment, which in turn supports their identity, health, wellbeing and culture. Human-induced climate change is affecting all of these aspects. In response, rights-based litigation is
content: Indigenous Peoples have stewardship of their physical environment, which in turn supports their identity, health, wellbeing and culture. Human-induced climate change is affecting all of these aspects. In response, rights-based litigation is increasing, including cases brought by Indigenous plaintiffs, for action to protect their health and wellbeing, cultural lands and natural resources. This article presents a case study from the Gomeroi/Kamilaroi Peoples’ Traditional Country in the Narrabri Forest region in Australia, where coal-seam gas mining leases were sought by the mining company Santos NSW and the New South Wales (NSW) State Government. The Gomeroi/Kamilaroi Peoples used Australia’s Native Title Act 1993, which recognises their pre-colonisation rights to the lands, to seek to reject the mining proposal. They invoked climate change impacts to detail the current and projected impacts. This case study focuses in detail on the climate-related impacts on the Gomeroi/Kamilaroi Peoples’ health and wellbeing and impacts on their Country. The case was novel in that climate change information was ruled admissible with regard to considerations under the Native Title Act 1993. The case was ultimately rejected by the National Native Title Tribunal. However, this provides a precedent for future cases. Furthermore, the 2025 ruling by the International Court of Justice that, under international human rights law, states have obligations to protect communities, ecosystems and the climate system. This is likely to shift future litigation outcomes.

title: Mesoporous nano-silica, nano-iron, and Ascophyllum nodosum extract enhance nutrient uptake and salt tolerance in maize
summary: Salinity restricts maize ( Zea mays L.) productivity by disrupting photosynthesis, nutrient acquisition, ionic balance, and redox homeostasis. This study investigated whether mesoporous nano-silica (MNS), nano-iron (Nano-Fe), and Ascophyllu
content: Salinity restricts maize ( Zea mays L.) productivity by disrupting photosynthesis, nutrient acquisition, ionic balance, and redox homeostasis. This study investigated whether mesoporous nano-silica (MNS), nano-iron (Nano-Fe), and Ascophyllum nodosum extract (ANE), applied alone or combined, could enhance maize tolerance to salinity. A factorial experiment was conducted in a completely randomized design under 0, 75, and 150 mM NaCl. Morphological, physiological, biochemical, gas-exchange, antioxidant, and stress-responsive molecular traits were evaluated. Salinity reduced plant height, fresh biomass, total chlorophyll, and net photosynthetic rate by 43.5%, 54.2%, 48.3%, and 60.7%, respectively, while increasing Na⁺ accumulation, osmotic stress, and oxidative damage. The combined MNS + Nano-Fe + ANE treatment provided the greatest protection, increasing plant height, fresh and dry biomass, and net photosynthetic rate by 47.8%, 72.0%, 101.9%, and 145.5%, respectively, relative to untreated plants at 150 mM NaCl. It improved chlorophyll retention, osmolyte and soluble-protein accumulation, antioxidant capacity, nutrient uptake, and ionic homeostasis while reducing malondialdehyde, hydrogen peroxide, and Na⁺ toxicity. Salinity induced ZmDREB2A , ZmHSP70 , ZmP5CS , ZmCAT1 , and ZmNHX1 , reflecting activation of stress signaling, osmotic adjustment, antioxidant defense, and ion transport. The combined treatment strengthened adaptive transcription under moderate salinity but moderated gene induction under severe stress, indicating improved homeostasis. Correlation analysis linked photosynthesis and nutrient accumulation positively with antioxidant and molecular responses and negatively with oxidative-stress markers. These findings demonstrate that integrating MNS, Nano-Fe, and ANE enhances maize salinity tolerance through photosynthetic protection, ion regulation, osmotic adjustment, reactive-oxygen-species detoxification, and molecular adaptation, offering a promising strategy for crop production in salt-affected soils.

title: Occurrence of potentially harmful phytoplankton and phycotoxins in eastern oysters within a coastal Alabama estuary
summary: Phytoplankton can affect estuarine organisms through nutrient depletion, physical damage, and phycotoxin production, yet exposure risks associated with changing phytoplankton assemblages remain poorly understood. The eastern oyster ( Crasso
content: Phytoplankton can affect estuarine organisms through nutrient depletion, physical damage, and phycotoxin production, yet exposure risks associated with changing phytoplankton assemblages remain poorly understood. The eastern oyster ( Crassostrea virginica ), a keystone estuarine species and sentinel of ecosystem health, has experienced unexplained mortality events that have been hypothesized to be linked to harmful phytoplankton exposure. Here, we assessed the occurrence of potentially harmful phytoplankton within a coastal Alabama estuary and phycotoxin presence within oyster tissues in conjunction with tracking of monthly oyster mortality, growth and condition from November 2022 through January 2024 at the Grand Bay Oyster Park in Grand Bay, Alabama. Taxa that may potentially cause harm through nutrient depletion, physical damage, and phycotoxin production were all observed during ~91%, ~57%, and ~22% of sampling events, respectively. Of the nine phycotoxins screened, only one, domoic acid (DA), was detected within oyster tissues, but in low levels (0.13 ± 0.01 mg toxin kg −1 shellfish meat; mean ± SEM). To our knowledge, this is the first documentation of DA in coastal Alabama oysters. Oyster growth, mortality and condition followed typical patterns for this region with no statistically detectable adverse effects associated with the observed phytoplankton or DA concentrations during the study period. These findings provide baseline information on harmful phytoplankton exposure and phycotoxin occurrence in a productive U.S. gulf coast oyster habitat and establish a reference for future environmental change.

title: Translating Science to Action: Findings from the 2026 Innovate4Cities Conference
summary: This report has been developed by the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate & Energy (GCoM) and the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat) based on findings from the 2026 Innovate4Cities Conference, held in Nairobi, Kenya,
content: This report has been developed by the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate & Energy (GCoM) and the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat) based on findings from the 2026 Innovate4Cities Conference, held in Nairobi, Kenya, from 21 to 24 June 2026. It is intended to inform science, policy, and practice – grounded in the Global Research and Action Agenda on Cities and Climate Change Science (GRAA).The report presents the key takeaways from the first Innovate4Cities Conference held on the African continent. It sets out the 10 priorities of the GRAA for 2026–2028, and reports on the takeaways, sessions, and findings from an in-person expert review of the IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Cities (SRCities), the 2026 AI x City Climate Action Hackathon, the Member State and Local Leaders roundtables, and the I4C26 Youth Team.Special thanks to the Knowledge and Creative Youth Teams for capturing content from the conference, used in this report. Their report can be found: https://doi.org/10.26188/34408185The authors have sought to ensure the accuracy of the material in this document, but they will not be liable for any ramifications incurred through the use of this report.To cite this report: Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy, UN-Habitat & University of Melbourne (2026). Translating Science to Action: Findings from the 2026 Innovate4Cities Conference. The University of Melbourne. Report. DOI: 10.26188/34704402

title: This study examined post-harvest losses (PHL) and their implications for food availability among smallholder fruit and vegetable farmers in Ethiopia's Oromia Region. The study was conducted in six kebeles of Adami Tulu Jido Kombolcha and Dugda woredas using a cross-sectional quantitative survey of 359 fruits and vegetable-producing households selected through multistage sampling method. Data were collected using structured questionnaires administered through KoboCollect App from December 2023 to March 2024. We assessed farm-level post-harvest loss (PHL) using the Aggregate Self-Reported Method, in which farmers reported quantities lost during harvesting and handling, transportation, storage, and marketing; we calculated percentage loss relative to the initial harvested quantity. The estimated producer-level losses were 11.84% for tomato, 8.62% for kale, and 13.81% for papaya. Regional-level PHL estimates were extrapolated by applying the farm-level loss rates estimated in this study to Oromia Region’s annual fruit and vegetable production data for 2013-2022. A deterministic 25% PHL-reduction scenario was used to estimate the quantity of produce that could theoretically be recovered and converted, using a dietary consumption benchmark into annual fruit-and-vegetable person-year supply equivalents. The analysis estimated cumulative fruit and vegetable PHL of 724,071.91 tons over the 2013-2022 period. Under the 25% PHL-reduction scenario, the estimated quantity of produce that could potentially be recovered varied across the study years. In 2022, the recovered quantity was equivalent to the annual fruit-and-vegetable consumption requirement of 832,444 people for one year (832,444.34 person-year equivalents), representing the highest annual estimate during the study period. When the annual estimates for 2013-2022 are summed, they amounted to approximately 3.31 million person-years. This cumulative estimate represented the aggregate annual food-supply equivalent generated over the ten years, expressed as the number of one-person annual fruit-and-vegetable consumption requirements that could theoretically be met by the recovered produce in each respective year. The findings indicated that reducing producer-level PHL could increase the quantity of fruit and vegetables potentially available for consumption, highlighting the importance of improved harvesting, handling, storage, transportation, and marketing practices among smallholder farmers. Key words: Post-harvest loss, smallholder farmers, fruit and vegetables, food availability, Ethiopia
